analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from paying less in jobs dominated by women or racial minorities than in equivalent jobs, and gives workers tools to sue.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate committee where it was introduced: it got one hearing in March 2010 and was never voted on by the committee or the full Senate before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal to pay workers less because they work in jobs dominated by women or racial minorities, when those jobs demand the same skills, effort, responsibility, and working conditions as better-paid jobs dominated by men. Current law only requires equal pay for people doing the exact same job, so jobs that take comparable training can pay very differently depending on who holds them. The bill would have let workers sue for back pay and damages, band together in class actions, get expert fees paid if they won, and report retaliation. It also would have required employers with 15 or more workers to report pay by job category, sex, race, and national origin to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, and applied the same rules to congressional and executive branch employees. The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate committee that handles labor law, got one hearing in March 2010, and expired when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers in occupations dominated by women, racial minorities, or national-origin groups — for example, childcare workers or nursing aides compared with better-paid equivalent jobs — who could recover unpaid wages and damages, sue as a class, and get expert fees covered if they win. Workers who discuss or compare wages gain explicit protection from firing or retaliation. Employers would also gain a clearer, EEOC-assisted compliance framework and pay data.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women and minority workers in lower-paid fields

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits paying lower wages in jobs dominated by women or minorities than in jobs dominated by men of another race or national origin when the jobs are 'equivalent' — dissimilar jobs whose requirements are equivalent in skills, effort, responsibility, and working conditions — going beyond the Equal Pay Act, which only covers unequal pay for the same work [S3].
It lets workers recover unpaid wages, plus compensatory and punitive damages, sue as a class, and recover expert-fee costs if they win [S3].
It makes it unlawful to fire or retaliate against an employee for opposing pay discrimination or for asking about, disclosing, or comparing wages [S2].

It requires employers with 15 or more employees to report wage rates by job classification along with the sex, race, and national origin of workers at each rate, giving regulators and the public data to spot patterns of pay discrimination [S3].
It directs the EEOC to research and teach employers and unions how to comply, and applies the same rules to congressional and executive branch employees [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would face new litigation exposure including compensatory and punitive damages, plus recordkeeping and annual wage reporting to the EEOC for employers with 15 or more employees. The bill bars compliance by cutting anyone's pay, so the cost of closing a gap falls on the employer's payroll.

drawbacks.text: The bill would extend liability beyond identical jobs to any two jobs whose 'requirements are equivalent' in skills, effort, responsibility, and working conditions, with the employer bearing the burden of proving any pay difference is job-related — a standard that invites litigation over hard-to-compare occupations and could raise costs for employers, including small ones subject to the rules once they pass 15 employees [S3].

Employers with 15 or more employees would have to compile and file pay reports broken down by sex, race, and national origin for every job classification, a compliance burden the EEOC could publish and sell to any member of the public, albeit with individual names removed [S3].

The bill adds compensatory and punitive damages on top of back pay for violations, and allows cases to proceed as class actions with expert fees reimbursed to winning plaintiffs, which opponents would argue increases the risk of large, expensive lawsuits even for unintentional pay gaps [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is substantial: roughly 78 cents on the dollar was the full-time pay gap cited in the bill's findings [S3], and this bill attacked the part of it that comes from paying female- and minority-dominated occupations less than male-dominated occupations of equivalent skill — the classic "comparable worth" approach that existing equal-pay law, which only compares identical jobs, cannot reach. It also gave workers real tools: class actions, expert fees, double damages in effect, and anti-retaliation protection for discussing wages. The costs are real and worth stating honestly: defining "equivalent jobs" across dissimilar occupations requires judgment calls that invite litigation, the pay-reporting requirement imposes paperwork on employers with 15 or more workers, and expanded damages raise business liability costs that some economists argue can make employers more cautious about hiring. But the bill was never debated or amended on the floor, so the country never got to weigh those tradeoffs; it died where it was introduced.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the Senate's labor committee, got one hearing, and then sat there until that Congress ended without ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the Fair Pay Act of 2009 on April 28, 2009, with 13 co-sponsors including Senator Edward Kennedy and Senator Bernie Sanders [S1].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the day it was introduced; that was the only formal step the full Senate ever took [S5].
The committee held a hearing on the bill on March 11, 2010 (printed as S.Hrg. 111-1135) but never voted to report it to the full Senate [S5].
No further action followed before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill expired [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off: they face no new pay-equity liability, no damages exposure, and no wage-reporting requirement, because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers facing no new pay-equity rules

for.what_they_did: Co-sponsored the bill, including Sen. Edward Kennedy, Sen. John Kerry, Sen. Russell Feingold, Sen. Bernie Sanders, Sen. Barbara Boxer, Sen. Patty Murray, Sen. Jeff Merkley, Sen. Patrick Leahy, Sen. Charles Schumer, Sen. Richard Durbin, and Sen. Daniel Akaka.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call record exists; the bill's only support on the record came from 13 senators, all Democrats plus Independent Bernie Sanders, and no senator is recorded as opposing it.

industries.note: The bill would expose employers to lawsuits and damages for pay gaps between jobs dominated by different groups, plus recordkeeping and annual pay reporting to the EEOC. Ordinary workers are on the winning side of that trade; the employer's cost is the enforcement mechanism for the worker's pay.

industries.industry: Payroll, HR compliance, and workforce analytics firms
industries.note: Mandatory wage reporting by job classification, sex, race, and national origin would create demand for software and consultants to compile it. This is a secondary effect of an enforcement bill, not its purpose.

Unions are barred from causing an employer to discriminate under the new rules, but their members would gain a wage-discrimination remedy and the bill protects workers' right to discuss pay. The bill does not entrench unions either way.
